utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellencies. I would like to hear about your decision first regarding Rule 90(E) that the witness evoked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber has decided to compel the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I don't believe we have translation -- interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said the Chamber had decided to compel the witness to answer the question. Mr. Stanisic, do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Could it be repeated, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We kindly ask the witness to approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the question be put again so that I can provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And in light of the submission of Mr. Zecevic, we'll continue in public session. But if you would like to answer the question in private session, please let us know in advance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Minister, did you when and in what way learn about the crime at Koricanske Stijene?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I learned of it two or three days after the event. I was informed by the assistant head of the centre in Banja Luka in charge of crime. I sent my instructions to him orally at first, and then in written form by way of dispatch. I sent my instructions to them in terms of what they were required to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The investigating judge, Mr. Jankovic, who was involved in the case, confirmed that he saw your telegram but that it simply disappeared from the file.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P03763 so that we can see whether it is the telegram in question which is then conveyed further by Chief Zupljanin in his own telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have the Serb version on the right. It states that he received a dispatch on the 31st of August with the following contents, and your name is cited. Is this the telegram you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Minister, according to what you know, were any measures taken at the time conditions permitting by the MUP, because, of course, you cannot address the issue of the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that the witnesses who were gravely wounded were found on the site and then transferred to the health centre in Banja Luka. I was informed that they were being guarded by members of the CSB Banja Luka so as to prevent any further harm from coming their way. I was also told that there was an on-site investigation which took some time and needed repeating because it was a very complex event and that the investigating judge and the public prosecutor were also informed and were taking part in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remind us of what you told us yesterday about how things work once the judiciary is involved.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess I need to repeat once again. As of the moment the investigating judge and the public prosecutor take over the case, the minister of the interior can be engaged only upon their request to gather information and carry out a different procedure that they requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether I or anyone else sent you any kind of instructions or suggestions to sabotage the investigation or that the state organs did not want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Objection. Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you expand why it was leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The question should have been just put: Did he send any instructions on this matter. Instead, Mr. Karadzic is suggesting alternatives and therefore putting words into the witness's mouth, or at least leading the witness to respond in a particular way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The definition of a leading question is one that suggests an answer, and Dr. Karadzic's question doesn't suggest an answer. The witness could equally answer it yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber sees the point where there's a part which is technically leading a little bit, but the Chamber is of the view we can go along with this question. Can you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one communicated with me in this regard. What I can say is that I had some indirect knowledge that the Presidency established some kind of commission which was supposed to go on site to assist. I believe it was the Defence Minister Bogdan Subotic who led the submission, although it included other people whose names I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Minister. Just one more question on the topic. Let me see if this is already in -- no, it's not in. Did the state bodies have an interest in not discovering the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: State bodies should have no interest in not identifying perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they exhibit any such tendency, did they provide such suggestions?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was in other people's heads, but what I do know is that there was no case similar to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Minister.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions of this witness at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, you were convicted of war crimes and crimes against humanity by this Tribunal on the 27th of March, 2013, after a two-and-a-half year trial and you were sentenced to 22 years of imprisonment; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By way of a trial judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in particular, you were convicted for your participation in a joint criminal enterprise that came into existence no later than the 24th of October, 1991, and continued through 1992, the objective of which was to permanently remove Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats from the territory of the planned Serbian state through the commission of crimes on a massive scale; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was no member of any joint criminal enterprise, and that is why I appealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether you accept your conviction or the findings against you. But that was, in fact, the findings of the Trial Chamber after your trial; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what one can read in the trial judgement. I assert it is incorrect and that is why I appealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber in your case also found that besides yourself, the joint criminal enterprise included, among others, Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik, Ratko Mladic, as well as a number of members of the RS MUP leadership, including Stojan Zupljanin, Predrag Jeseric, Andrija Bjelosevic, Simo Drljaca, Malko Koroman, and others; isn't that correct? That's what they found.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can find it in the judgement. But I assert I was no part of any enterprise and that is why I appealed. I still await a decision of the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the crimes against non-Serbs of which you were convicted were perpetrated in 20 municipalities, including Bijeljina, Kljuc, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Vlasenica, Zvornik, Banja Luka, Brcko, Pale, and Vogosca; isn't that correct? That's what the Trial Chamber found.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to show it to me so I can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 25895 on the screen and turn to page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, I only have it in English. I don't know if that's going to cause any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that we don't have translation at all on the part of the Tribunal or it was not uploaded on the -- onto the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may be of assistance to the Trial Chamber, the translation of the judgement is still pending I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- afraid, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Perhaps, Your Honour, at this point I just direct Your Honours' attention to the relevant paragraph in the Trial Judgement; that is, trial judgement paragraph 927, which finds Mr. Stanisic guilty of crimes committed in 20 municipalities, and the municipalities are dealt with throughout the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, the crimes that you were convicted of included persecution, killings, torture, unlawful detention, forcible transfer, plunder, imposition of discriminatory measures, wanton destruction of towns and villages, as well as the willful destruction of religious institutions; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I had no occasion to read my judgement because it still has not been translated. I am familiar with some of its parts, working on my appeal with the Defence team. However, off the cuff I cannot recall many of the things you say. I would really like to be able to follow. You enumerate many things and it's difficult to follow. I apologise. If you put a summary question, I can't provide specific answers. Could we go one thing at a time so that we can discuss it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At this stage I'm simply having you confirm what the trial chamber found in the case against you. If you're unable to confirm that those were what you were convicted of, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, I think it'd maybe be best just to admit these excerpts from the judgement into the -- into evidence and Your Honours can review them at your leisure, since this witness is not prepared to confirm them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think his comment that he hasn't received the translation is a -- fair enough. So why don't we just go on. Would you like to tender the judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Not the judgement. I took out some excerpts here, I think it's 19 or 20 pages, and that would allow the Trial Chamber to take into consideration what this witness was convicted of during the course of his trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's fair enough, Mr. President. I think it goes to his credibility and it's fair to do that, but it should be limited, so I'd like to have a chance to review the excerpts and we'll see if we can agree on exactly what should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you could identify the part that you mean to tender, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps we could just mark it for identification now and can I look at that maybe during the break or sometime in the near future and maybe work with Defence counsel on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll deal with it when you tender that part later on. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecution from the 16th to the 21st of July, 2007. Do you stand by the answers you gave during that interview?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by each and every answer of mine. If you want me to be more specific, I'm afraid you'll have to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly. And I might do that. But first of all I'd like to ask you, and I understand that you haven't had a chance to read your entire judgement in your language, but you recall that in assessing your criminal responsibility the trial chamber in your case took into consideration that you shared a close relationship with Radovan Karadzic from at least June 1991. That's what the Trial Chamber found; isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even without being able to look at the judgement, I claim it was improperly established, and that is why I appealed the decision of the trial chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I ask, your Excellencies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You overlapped. Could you repeat, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I ask the question: Is the acquaintance with me or close relation with me criminal act?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not a proper intervention, Mr. Karadzic. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, just while we have a pause in --- I wanted to just call to the attention of Mr. Olmsted since he is -- this is his first time here and make sure there's no misunderstanding, and that's simply that the time of the direct examination has been reported to us as three hours and 17 minutes. So I assume that following our practice, Mr. Olmsted will, instead of the five hours that the Chamber gave him, will now have three hours and 17 minutes for his cross-examination. So I thought I should make that clear at the outset so that he wasn't under any misapprehension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you are aware of that practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I actually was operating under the assumption that I -- I would have five hours. The reason being is the number of general assertions made by Mr. Stanisic during his direct examination, which are generally the ones that are contained within his 92 ter statement so there really isn't -- not much of a difference between the two. And in order to address those generalisations, I will unfortunately have to be showing the witness a number of documents, and showing documents will take time and therefore I would request that at least the Trial Chamber will take into consideration granting me the five hours that it originally granted me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Olmsted, the Chamber will stick to its practice. You'll be given the same amount of time that the Defence has spent. But as -- as always, if good cause is shown at the end of your cross, the Chamber is minded to consider to allow you some extension.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: By way of example of your relationship with Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 31796 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, just one thing to say. When you speak I receive interpretation in my earphones, and you seem to be rather loud and then I have a problem hearing interpretation since we are relatively close. I'm unable to follow interpretation. You speak rather loudly, and then I have my interpretation interrupted. Perhaps it could be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll definitely take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Maybe there's an overlap in his microphone -- we'll take a look into that. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this is a telephone intercept of a conversation between you and Mr. Karadzic on 12 June 1991, and this was admitted in your case. And in this intercept, we see that Karadzic called you at your home. He referred to you as Mico. You talked a little bit about your son. And then Mr. Karadzic - we might have to go to the next page - invited to you his home. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to see the context. Can you go back to the previous page? I'd like to see the whole conversation. Mr. Prosecutor, at that time, I was a secretary of the Sarajevo SUP. Whatever problems there were with regard to the persons who provided security in town or, rather, who were entitled to security, party leaders, their assistants and other VIPs who were to be protected by the ministry, I, as the secretary of the SUP, i.e., the secretariat, looked after their security and everything that happened in the area. At home, I had a special telephone, a special line, as we call it, that anybody could dial and call me if there were any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And during this telephone conversation, you addressed Mr. Karadzic as Mr. President. Were you referring to his position as president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I addressed Izetbegovic and Kljujic. They liked to be called that and it was also a matter of courtesy and it was not a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we don't have any objection. But I note that on the subject line of the English translation there is an error, so perhaps that can be revised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should read "Mico Stanisic" instead of "Milan Babic." Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6624, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness wanted to see the context. We can see the first and the last page, but that's not the entire context. I want to see the context. I want to see it, if nobody else does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's -- of two pages. That's all. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that you were on the initiative committee of the democratic party of BiH. What you didn't mention was that you were, for a period of time in 1990, on the SDS Main Board, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a misinterpretation, Mr. Prosecutor. The SDS did not exist in 1990. Initially the party was established as the democratic party of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It changed its name on the eve of the assembly, which happened on the 12th of July in Skenderija, in Sarajevo. As I told you yesterday, I don't know the reasons. I can only speculate because I was not a member of the body that discussed the change of the name. The party was supposed to be led by Professor Kecmanovic. I was a member of the Initiative Board because on that day it was established under the name the Serbian Democratic Party, and that's all can I tell you and that's all I witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I appreciate your willingness to give full answers, Mr. Stanisic. But given my limited time, a simple yes or no would be fine and if necessary a short explanation. You do not need to repeat what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 21548 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Hasn't been released, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. There's a brief delay here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, while waiting for this document, I'm going to put to that in 1991 you were still a member of the SDS and that is why you addressed Mr. Karadzic in that last intercept as "Mr. President"?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 18874 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is an invitation to SDS members employed in government ministries and other republican organisations to the session of the SDS Deputies Club.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see that your name is listed under number 29 as secretary of the city secretariat of interior. That's the position you held from May 1991 until February 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I occupied that position. Mr. Prosecutor, these are the people who were appointed to the positions that were given to the SDS when there were negotiations between the HDZ and the SDS on the distributions of posts. I explained that yesterday. When there were negotiations about the distribution of posts between the HDZ, the SDA, and the SDS in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was intended to result in the proportional representation of the ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time, there was a coalition of the SDA, the SDS, and HDZ, and that coalition was in power in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here that those were members of the SDS. Not interpretation. In the translation. Which is why Mr. Olmsted may have been misled. The translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not the interpretation, the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if -- with the leave of Your Honour, if the interpreters could read the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the interpreters do not do that. Mr. Stanisic, could you read out the title of this document, aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "To the Session of the Serbian Democratic Party Group," and that group was made up of the MPs in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, "invite the following cadre of the SDS employed in the government ministries and other republic organisations." This means that the posts were given to the SDS and they were given to the officials from the ranks of the Serbian people which doesn't have to mean -- and I claim that at least 60 per cent of the names that you can see here were of the people who were non-partisan who were not members of any party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, if you read that like this, it's very difficult for us to distinguish what is in the document and what is yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I thought I would be of assistance. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I leave it at that. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, was this admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6625, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have now 65 ter 21548 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I'd like to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cadres are not translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like you to raise in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a technical issue. And this is an error on the part of the translation service. I don't want to waste my time on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic gave his interpretation about this. And then if there's an issue with its written translation, you can raise it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the issue is with the oral translation. The word "cadre" was translated where the word "member" appeared in the English. To us, understanding it, "cadre" and "member" seem to be the same. But as what Dr. Karadzic is trying to say is that it has a different meaning and another word should have been used by the interpreters when they were translating what Mr. Stanisic read. So it might be useful to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When Mr. Stanisic read the document, it was noted in the transcript: "Invite the following cadre of the SDS employed...," so what that means could be clarified with the witness by Mr. Karadzic in his re-examination. He didn't -- it was not translated as "members."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think Dr. Karadzic is saying that the term "cadre" is also wrong, that that's not correct translation for that term that's used in Serbian. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But then that's not a subject to interfere with Mr. Olmsted's cross and in wasting time. He has other means to raise it and properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you've told us to, when we have an interpretation error in court, to raise it -- that he's entitled to raise it at that time so that we don't proceed on a false premise for the rest of the examination. That what's he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Still, I don't follow. What should be the proper word for this "cadre"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic doesn't believe that that's a proper interpretation of the word in Serbian that appeared on the document. "Cadre" to me means the same thing as member, and he says that what's expressed in the document is the people who occupied the post allocated to the SDS, not people who were members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure this "cadre" means a member. But, yes, Mr. Karadzic, could you expand on your reasons? What's wrong with this translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, almost nobody on the list was an SDS member and it --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- appears that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you stick to your meaning of "cadre" in the issue of translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Cadre" in the Serbian means or denotes somebody who was nominated by the party, not that it is its member. The way it is interpreted translated in English, it appears that they are members of the SDS and they are not members of the SDS they are the cadre of the Serbian people. [In English] Not members of the SDS, cadre of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic made it clear that he was not a member and he explained it. I think we have heard sufficient explanation about this. You may raise it in your re-examination again, if necessary. Please continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, on the screen we have a document that is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Tieger switch off his microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We have a list of the SDS Main Committee members. And do you see your name under number 19?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6626, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: While you were RS MUP minister in 1992, you followed the policies of the SDS Presidency, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not the Presidency of the SDS. Please. If you want to refer to a place where I said something, when it comes to the SDS policy, the party establishes that through the laws that it passes as a majority party. I functioned within the framework of the Law on Internal Affairs which was the product of the SDS policy. And it is true that by applying provisions of the law in my work I observed the decisions because I believed that there was nothing incriminating there because the Law on Internal Affairs in the Republika Srpska was copied from the law of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina with slight changes because the communism had disappeared, there was no socialist party etc, but in essence it was a copy of that law. For me that was the policy, which means that the policy was established in the assembly and what was clearly adopted in the assembly was also adopted by me. Everything that was within the framework of the constitution and laws as a product of the SDS policy. I observed that, I complied with all those things, and I did not notice any discrimination either in the constitution or the laws that were passed by the assembly whose members were also members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P1105 on the screen. And if we could turn to page 15 of the English; page 16 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now during the 22nd Session of the RS Assembly on the 23rd of November 1992, you stated: "I as a man have followed policies of the SDS Presidency and our deputies in the former state. I have always followed these policies. Those who want to separate me from them, I will always be with them until it is shown that their wishes an intentions differ from those of their people. Those who want to separate me from that are making a big mistake. I will not allow that even if it costs me my life, let alone a ministerial post." That is a level of dedication that you expressed at the 22nd Session, Assembly Session. Isn't it correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely the answer that I provided a little while ago, Your Honours, and I emphasised the framework which is provided for by the laws that were passed by the MPs, this is what I complied with. There is nothing discriminatory in those laws. I respected decisions passed by the members of the Presidency. You saw in my requests where I ask that problems be resolved, where I received support, and for as long as things were like that, I said I would comply with everything. That's how things were. Whenever I sensed that something went beyond that framework, I left the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Stanisic, I ask you to try to keep your answers short and focused on my question. Now, this same level of dedication to SDS policies was shared throughout the RS MUP, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policy, that was formulated through the laws that were passed by the assembly, and its members were mostly members of the SDS, was implemented by the Ministry of Interior through the implementation of its missions and tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could quickly look at 65 ter 18389.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is a report by CSB Sarajevo on certain political security aspects in the area dated 15 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see towards the bottom of the English that the CSB Sarajevo reports that the SDS had its support primarily in the police. That was the case, wasn't it, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only based on the laws passed by the assembly. That was available to us. The laws were publicised as a result of the work of the SDS MPs, and those laws for us were the framework with which -- within which we functioned. And I told you just a minute ago what I thought about laws in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, this is a five-page and pretty dense document which I am trying to read as we go along, and he only put to him one phrase from the document which he read out. I don't think there is a basis to admit the entire document. But we may not have any objection once we have had a chance to assess it, it's -- what the whole thing is. But on principle, I think he's put to the witness the part of the document that he wanted and it doesn't need to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to add anything, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Except for it, Your Honours, that we're tendering this because it goes to the witness's credibility with regard to the issue of SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the issue is whether to admit this page or in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We would want it to be admitted in its entirety so that it can be put into its context, but I'll leave that to Your Honours' discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit only the page shown to the witness. Shall we assign the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6627, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, during the 1991/1994 period, it was Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik who determined SDS policy. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic was the president of the SDS; whereas, Mr. Krajisnik was the Speaker of the SDS Assembly. And it is true that they were the most responsible people. Now, as to what they did and what kind of relationship they had is something that I can't comment upon because it would be pure speculation on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 65 ter 25865. And if we could have page 73 of the English version, page 41 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, this is from your interview back in 2007. And we can see that you stated the SDS policy was run by Karadzic and Krajisnik. Further along you say no individual could influence their policy, not even the deputies in parliament. Further along you say we were, so to say, with them but we were below them or under them. Sir, when you refer to the word "we," you're referring to the Bosnian Serb authorities, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Prosecutor, this is what I just told you. They were the highest organs. Krajisnik was the speaker of the parliament and Mr. Karadzic was the president of the party, and it was only normal that they were the most responsible for the creation of the policy because one of them would become the president of the state and the other one was the speaker of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the regional and municipal Crisis Staffs were subordinate to the RS Presidency; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a War Presidency at the level of the republic and there were presidencies at the levels of the regions and municipalities. And obviously along the line of subordination, bodies at the lower level were accountable to the bodies at the higher level.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the RS Presidency both verified the decisions of the regional and municipal Crisis Staffs as well as the composition of those bodies; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, in fact, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik implemented SDS policies through the regional and municipal Crisis Staffs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I would just like to add that from the moment when one of them became the president of the republic and the other one the speaker of the assembly, they pursued state policy. And I already said how anywhere in the world parties defined their policies through parliament because Krajisnik and Karadzic could not be beyond the law. But through members of parliament, they could influence the profile of the laws in parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's quickly turn to page 259 of your interview. That's in the English. Page 139 of the B/C/S. And in the English version, I'm referring to the very bottom where you stated during your interview: "Those Crisis Staffs performed the initiative of national parties ...," that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. All national parties in extraordinary circumstances or when the war was going on had these Crisis Staffs but through the state organs. As I said a moment ago, they could exercise this control through laws and bylaws that were passed in the assembly. I'm sorry. I cannot speculate in terms of whether somebody did something individually. I am telling you about what I knew and what my view was, how a state should function.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When Prime Minister Djeric attempted to regulate the Crisis Staffs in April 1992, Mr. Karadzic prevented him and warned him that the organisation of local self-government is not within the competence of the government but in the competency of the Presidency; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Territorial organisation and the establishment of the territorial organisation was under the assembly; and in an emergency, then the Presidency can replace it but inform the assembly. And that's what our Djeric did. And now this instruction, what Crisis Staffs should be like. That was withdrawn the very next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, to clarify this issue, why don't we turn to the next page in the English. And you stated during your interview: "So on 24th of April, the government tried by means of an institution or instruction or guide-lines to reorganise those Crisis Staffs. However, the Presidency headed by Mr. Karadzic warned Mr. Djeric that the organisation of local self-government is not in the competence of the government but in the competence of the assembly or the Presidency until the assembly is constituted," and that his views were not in line with that of the members of the Presidency. And then you go on and say that this was formulated in a letter and down the road the War Presidencies were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: "But" -- and this is what you said during your interview: "But, in essence, nothing changed." That's what you said during your interview and you stand by that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by every word that I uttered. That's the way it was; that was the information that I received at the government. It wasn't only I. The entire government did. Then this instruction with withdrawn on the organisation of the Crisis Staffs. And later on, Presidencies were established. Actually first it was commissioners, I think, and then Presidencies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, could you come closer to the microphone when you speak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that line 12 is correctly typed out. I think the witness said "reorganisation" and here it says "organisation." And also in the interview, it says "redefining Crisis Staffs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, can you assist us on this -- on this one? Did you say "organisation" or "reorganisation"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to change the organisation that existed until then. To have certain changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, just having a discussion with Mr. Tieger, and I would like to tender some of these portions from his interview. We loaded them, though, as one, the whole -- the whole interview, and I think obviously we just want the extracts. So with your leave what I'll do at the end of his testimony is I will just extract them, send them to the Defence, they can review them and make sure that they're happy with extract, and then we tender them at that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we'll admit only those pages shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, that's fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know that I have no standing about the documents in this case and that is not my comment. I just wanted to make sure that my learned friend in the future when he refers to something, may we please have the Serbian version on the screen also for the fairness to the witness so he can read what -- what Mr. Olmsted is referring to. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. I meant to come to that issue. Yes. Please bear that in mind, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. And, Mr. President, I wasn't aware that the B/C/S wasn't keeping up with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said I meant to come to that issue. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karadzic exercised control over you as a MUP official, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic was president of the republic, and his authority is clearly defined by the constitution and a series of other laws.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could Mr. Olmsted specify whether he is referring to an official before the war or when he was a minister or, rather, during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm meaning the whole period, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that Mr. Zepinic and Mr. Mandic told you that they had consent to offer you the position of secretary of the SUP. That consent was provided by Mr. Karadzic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that they had Karadzic's consent. That is not controversial. That is to say that they had agreed that I would accept this position of secretary, so that was this official talk. The one that Mandic conducted with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And be -- between your two terms as minister of the interior, between 1992 -- after you left in 1992 and before you were reappointed in 1994 or the end of 1993, you served as advisor to Mr. Karadzic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just -- actually, at that moment when I was relieved of my duties, when I held no post, I went to Belgrade. Then Mr. Karadzic issued a decision stating that I was advisor so that I would not be subjected to mobilisation, otherwise I should have to go out as a soldier. I insisted on that, that I should be free of any obligation towards the army because, after all, I worked a lot there on getting rid of criminal groups, and I certainly exposed my life, well, if I were to come as a soldier into that area. But I was not in Republika Srpska. With my family, I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could quickly have 65 ter 22032 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a letter from you dated 7 April 1993, and you sign it as republican advisor for domestic politics. And in it you refer to an order by the president of the RS. You sent this document, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not my signature. I don't know who sent this. This is not my signature. Take a look at this. Compare it. I really don't know. This is the first time I see this. As a matter of fact, it doesn't even say "for," and then a different signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic was behind your appointment to your second term as minister of the interior, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But let's see whether the witness agrees whether he was a republican advisor for domestic politics. Do you agree you were in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I received a decision on appointment in order to be protected from mobilisation and from being sent to the front line, because I held no position at that point in time. But I was in Belgrade with my family. In fact, I did not have any job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, with that answer I would tender this for purposes of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, since there's no authentication of the document, Mr. President, we would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I -- I actually withdraw my -- my offering initially. I tender it for all purposes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The basis upon which we can admit it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it certainly goes to credibility. But we submit that it is an authentic document. Obviously the witness claims that he didn't sign it, but it is -- there is no challenge as to its authenticity on a basis of where it came from or its provenance, so we would tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether witness confirmed that he was in that position at all. Do you have any other evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, that he was an advisor to the Presidency? Yes, we do. I would direct your attention to P1382 which is the 36th Session of the RS Assembly, page 51 of the English, in which Prime Minister Lukic identifies Mr. Stanisic as advisor to the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your answer, Mr. Stanisic, was not clear to me. Do you agree you were at one point of time a republican advisor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, formally yes; but in fact, no, because in that period of time I lived in Belgrade with my family. This document has nothing whatsoever to do with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will mark it for identification until the time that the Chamber would be satisfied with its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI'd P6628, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Karadzic was behind your appointment to your second term as minister of the interior, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a short answer because this is rather more complex. It is certain that Karadzic gave his support there because after I left problems cropped up again in the territory of Republika Srpska, and the professional part of the Ministry of Interior insisted that they bring me back because the person who became minister did not really know anything about the interior, and then these para groups started returning, and then crime again was in full sway and they insisted that I come back, and indeed I did come back. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm not asking for the reasons of your reappointment, but Mr. Karadzic's authorisation was -- was necessary for your appointment, wasn't it? He had to approve it.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I said that. It is certain that Mr. Karadzic agreed to that because ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in July 1994, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik removed you from the position of minister of the interior because you were collecting information about financial crimes committed by them and members of their family; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that in July 1994 I was removed and that precisely shows my position of principle; namely, that I just followed the law, not any individual, even if that individual was an official. And that is why I clashed not only with Krajisnik but I think with the vice-premier too and a few members of the government. As for Mr. Karadzic, I held it against him because he stood by them and I was dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to 65 ter 25865. This is your interview again. And I want page 171 of the English on, page 95 of the B/C/S. And we see that you stated during your interview: "So when Karadzic and Krajisnik found out that their brothers and the people who were around them were being interviewed, immediately organised for me to be removed from the position."

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll try again. Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have that passage before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. It's in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I mean the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I believe it's -- I mean, as I don't read B/C/S, I can't confirm, but I was told that it's on page 95. Yes. And I think it is. If you look at the first answer given by Mr. Stanisic, it's -- it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During your interview, Mr. -- could you hear? Yes. Mr. Stanisic, during your interview, which is in front of you, you said: "So when Karadzic and Krajisnik found out that their brothers and the people who were around them were being interviewed, immediately organised for me to be removed from the position." That was the case, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't change anything a moment ago. That's the way it was. Well, it had to do with white-collar crime. And you can see from my behaviour in 1992 towards another member of the Presidency. As soon as I noticed that there were reasons for violating the law, I ordered action regardless of who was involved. And that confirms that my attitude was only professional, even if this were the speaker of the assembly, the president of the state, a colleague, or anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And around the time of your removal in 1994, you told Mr. Karadzic that he tried to instill into you the members of the government and members of the Presidency are supposed to be untouchables to the MUP; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that for me? It was a very long question and it was not precise enough for me to give an accurate answer. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly. Around the time of your removal in 1994, you told Mr. Karadzic that he tried to instill in you that members of the government and members of the Presidency are supposed to be untouchables to the MUP, didn't you? You had that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was this session of the government and Mr. Karadzic was present too. And Krajisnik. And I represented the interests of the Ministry of Interior. And 90 per cent of the others were on the other side. They were against my position. In all fairness, I have to be frank: Mr. Karadzic attacked me more because I made this public in the media, and I did that on purpose so that no one could exercise any influence over me in terms of whether I should be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please start this sentence again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, could you repeat from your -- from -- where you said "and I did that on purpose."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On purpose, this level of investigation attained, about white-collar crime. These persons that I mentioned in the previous part of my statement. I stated this to the media on purpose, probably, because it wasn't only Krajisnik. There were four or five members of the government, too. The vice-premier as well. And I knew that an attempt would be made to hush this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's turn to this interview, page 312 of the English; page 169 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see here in the third paragraph, you state -- at least in the English version: "I told to Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik and other present members: They tried to instill into me that the members of the government and members of the Presidency are supposed to be untouchables to the MUP." And then further up --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are unable to find the reference in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps could we turn to the next page, see if it's there. No, I think it's -- if we can go back to the previous page, I think it's there. And I see at the very top it seems to be at where it references Karadzic and Krajisnik. But perhaps Mr. Zecevic can help me with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it's the first paragraph of the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So during your interview, you stated that you told Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik as well as others present at that session that they tried to instill into you that members of the government and members of the Presidency are supposed to be untouchables to the MUP. And then further on you said during your interview: "And I openly told Mr. Karadzic that he had sided with the criminals. At that very moment I was practically relieved of my duties." Or "my position," I'm sorry. And that continues onto the next page. That's correct, isn't it? Mr. Stanisic, you just have to verify that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And it's contained in the minutes from the government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this a compilation of several interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, the interview took place over several days and so it is quite large, and what I will do is I will identify the pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we admit them as we go back and add the pages. So shall we assign a number now for this interview.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6629, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you have any objection to admit those pages referred to -- referred to and confirmed by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll admit all those pages, and we'll add the pages as we go by. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And just for the record, I have been informed that P6624 has been -- the translation has now been fixed and uploaded and it can be admitted fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P1082 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, yesterday you testified that you were a member of the Council of Ministers of the Serbian -- or the Bosnian Serb Assembly. And you attended their meetings; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the ministerial council as a minister without portfolio. And I believe there was only one meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we actually have records of two meetings in evidence in this case, and they both mention you as attending them. Do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not dispute that. But can you show it to me, please. Can you show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'll show you the first one for the sake of time. And this -- these are the minutes from the first meeting of the ministerial council held on 11 January 1992. And if we could turn to page 2, it was concluded that the priorities springing from the declaration of the promulgation of the republic of the Serbian people of BH "included the defining of ethnic territory, establishment of government organs in the territory, and the economic dis-empowerment of the current authorities in the socialist republic of BiH." These were the priorities of the council of ministers, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it but I presume it was so if it is in the document. I didn't chair the meeting. I told you I did not have a portfolio and, thus, I had nothing to do with this particular topic. In any case, I think it was following the results of the arbitration commission and the negotiations before that for the Serb side to organise its own territory, its own area. I think this is a consequence of the level the negotiations have reached in terms of dealing with the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was just putting things on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you refer to arbitration commission, you're not referring to the Cutileiro negotiations, are you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Even before the Cutileiro commission, there was the Badinter commission which participated in trying to deal with the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina from a legal standpoint. Cutileiro approached it from a political angle under the umbrella of the European Commission in order to deal with the economic crisis -- sorry, the constitutional crisis which was created in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It came as a result of the breakup of the only internationally recognised state in that area, which was the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could just turn to the next page, we see that you were at this meeting assigned to a Working Group to deal with issues regarding the organisation and scope of national security; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me read it first. So which paragraph is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I find in paragraph 4. So an analysis had to be done to assess the situation by the group. But the group never met or did anything in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on the screen P1083.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, on the 11th of February 1992 you attended a meeting in Banja Luka that was also attended by a number of the members of the Bosnian Serb leadership of the BiH MUP; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see from the minutes of that meeting that after Stojan Zupljanin convened the meeting you were the first to speak, and you informed those present that the position of the Council of Ministers at the last session was that in territories in the SRBiH, which are under Serbian control, that control must be felt. You were advocating the priorities of the Council of Ministers, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you misinterpreted this paragraph. I did not say "control." I said that in such parts where the MUP had Serb personnel performing the tasks and duties of the Ministry of the Interior, that they should conscientiously go about doing their jobs so that such authority is felt in the area. The problem by the time was that certain guards were organised and people started taking care of their own security in villages. My line of thinking was that we should try to show to the people that the authorities were still functioning and that it could be felt in the field. It was not about any kind of control.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that there's another misunderstanding because of the translation of the document which, in the English, reads "control." In the original, it is stated as "the presence of authority."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we ask the witness to read out the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, could you read out the first sentence underneath your name.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the position of the Council of Ministers during the last session, which I mentioned a moment ago, is that in the territory inside the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the whole republic, which is under Serb authority, because there were parts where Serb personnel were in the majority and they were in charge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We want to hear the translation. Without adding explanation, just read out the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I thought you were looking for an answer. "It is the position of the council ever ministers adopted at its last session is that in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is under Serb territory, that authority must be felt," that it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you further stated at this meeting: "Work has to be done by the organisation of the Serbian MUP starting from the municipal and regional levels up to the Serbian ministry. The Serbian personnel in the MUP must provide the means to strengthen and supply the Serbian MUP ..." You assigned this task to the Serbian personnel, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly, we can turn the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: B/C/S, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In B/C/S, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we stay in -- in the English on -- on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I conveyed that position which had to do with the level reached in terms of re-establishing the constitutional order in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At that position was in the -- in the area where Serbs are in the majority, it would be a Serb entity. Where there are Muslims, it would be a Muslim entity. And with the ongoing negotiations, there was supposed to be a transformation of the MUP in terms of the regional Security Services Centres.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another objection in terms of the translation. It is stated that Serb -- the assets of the MUP would be distributed proportionally, not equally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add, Professor Koljevic who participated in the negotiations conveyed it to us that way, that there was agreement between the Muslim, Serb, and Croat side, under the auspices of the international community, that the transformation would develop in that direction. So I simply conveyed what I heard in terms of further developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said that an agreement had been reached under the auspices of the international community. Which agreement are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, those negotiations did not happen in one day. I was discussing the level reached as part of those negotiations. There was no agreement yet. The Cutileiro Plan was signed, I believe, on the 18th. I'm speculating. In any case, it was later. But I was discussing the level of discussion reached at those negotiations. That is what I had in mind. I wasn't discussing any signed agreements, simply the level that was reached and what direction any future transformation was supposed to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You, as you said yesterday, closely followed the Cutileiro negotiations. You were aware that they didn't even commence until the 13th of February, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, a moment ago I said that there were different negotiations about how Bosnia-Herzegovina was to be transformed. It ran in parallel with the negotiations concerning the transformation of Yugoslavia. Cutileiro had arrived by that time and he was included by that time as well, as well as Mr. Vance and a number of other representatives. I don't recall them all. The arbitration commission, legally speaking, once we informed that the Serbs intended to create Republika Srpska and were forwarded appropriate documents, we were waiting for their answer. Bosnia had already submitted their request to have Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised as independent, and the arbitration commission provided their opinion, number four, I believe, stating that the request on the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be accepted because there was Republika Srpska in existence, since they had seen our documents. They were sent by our side, that is to say, by the assembly Speaker Krajisnik, and they proposed how things would go from that point on. They didn't say that it was something outside the scope of the law but they simply cited the reasons why Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be recognised as a whole. I was discussing the results of the overall negotiation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, that was a very long answer to a very short question, as to when the Cutileiro negotiations began. Please, I ask you to keep your answers a little bit shorter, and I think you can. Now, you testified yesterday that the barricades incident in Sarajevo on the 2nd of March, 1992, was a reaction to a killing at a wedding and that your involvement under the instructions of Minister Delimustafic was to use your influence to have the barricades removed. Mr. Stanisic, in fact, you participated in the barricades incident not as a member of the BiH MUP but as a member of the SDS Crisis Staff for Sarajevo; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, first of all, you mis-formulated the question. You said that I was to wield my influence so that they could remove the barricades. It was not only my influence. It was the work of different MUP members from all sides. There were double barricades, Muslim and Croat as well. I was only one of the people working on it. I don't know what it was you wanted me to say. I lost the gist of your question. Can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'll show you a document, D3803. This is a document tendered into evidence by Mr. Karadzic. And it's a BiH MUP public security memorandum regarding the barricades incident. It's dated 13 March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 4 in the English, page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You are listed as one of the SDS Crisis Staff members who engaged in the barricades incident. That was the case, wasn't it, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time, and it is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 10752 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a BiH MUP state security report dated 6 March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 3 of the English, page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see towards the bottom, it states: "A number of active and reserve employees of the BiH MUP of Serb nationality were also directly included in the organising of the barricades and in other activities." That's referring to you, Mr. Stanisic, as well as Momcilo Mandic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true. Momcilo Mandic led a group of Serbian personnel in charge of removing them. The State Security Service is not familiar with the public security service activities. They may have seen Momcilo Mandic somewhere along the way as the problem was being dealt with. But this is incorrect. The only correct thing is that we did take part on the second day trying to tackle the problem. Ultimately, we made a great contribution on both sides of the MUP to have the barricades removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we go a little bit further up in this document, we see that the report concludes that the barricades were not a spontaneous reaction to the murder of Nikola Gardovic. That's correct, isn't it? It wasn't spontaneous? In other words, it was planned.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I can only tell you what I know. Not only that he was killed. The problem was also that the perpetrator was being sheltered in the Stari Grad police station, under protection, where there were no members of the Ministry of Interior who were Serb. He was sheltered there. He was hiding on the premises of the Stari Grad police station. It came out and it contributed to the problem of the wedding ceremony member being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And barricades were established not only in Sarajevo but in surrounding municipalities; isn't that correct? Ilijas and other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speculate with regard to the rest, but I am positive it was so in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection for this page being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to tender the entire document. It -- I don't have obviously the time to go through the entire document with this witness, but it is relevant and explains the state of affairs with regard to the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is a ten-page document which contains a lot of contentious information about these events during a period in March, and I think it would be unfair to admit it without the witness being able to comment on those events. So those portions which he commented on we don't have any problem with, but it's as far as we think it should go and we think that's been our practice with documents of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may. We've heard the witness's evidence regarding his interpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was waiting for the translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- to be completed. Yes, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. We've heard the witness's evidence regarding this incident and how he interpreted it. This is a document from the BiH MUP which Mr. Stanisic has testified was the one that sent him out to the barricades to resolve -- help resolve the issues, and I think it's appropriate for Your Honours to have the full context of this issue in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Can the Prosecutor show us where it is stated that he was sent by the state security to the barricades. This document comes from the head of state security. Mr. Stanisic sent -- he was tasked to do so by the MUP, not by the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit the cover page and the page shown to the witness. Shall we assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6630, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P5602 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'm going to show you, Mr. Stanisic, the intercept of the telephone conversation that you had with Mr. Karadzic that -- on the 2nd of March 1992, and you reviewed this yesterday. But if we could turn to page 2, we can see -- and I think in the English version it's beginning towards the bottom. Before Mr. Jovanovic handed the telephone over to you, he tells Mr. Karadzic: "We want to remove the barricades. We've reached an agreement and that's all." And Mr. Karadzic responds: "What's that all about, what they agreed on?" Mr. Jovanovic then tells Mr. Karadzic: "Just what we wanted. There won't be any negotiations with Europe about either sovereign or non-sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina until the parties agree on that one." Mr. Stanisic, BiH sovereignty was the reason for the barricades, not the killing of a wedding. The killing at the wedding was simply a trigger?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. If I may clarify. The reason for the barricades was exclusively the incident which had taken place. It is a fact, though, that both political sides, the Serb and Muslim side, wanted to profit from it as politicians do. But it was not within our remit. The only important thing for us was to have the barricades removed without casualties. It is true, though, that later on both sides formulated their positions - the Serb side and the Muslim side - to enter into negotiation. However, I can only speculate as to that. I do know they were engaged in it. I don't think either the Serb or Muslim side organised the barricades. It was when politics became involved that the stakes were raised, but this is how I see the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could look at P5612. And if we could turn to page 2 of the B/C/S; page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
