utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, this is a telephone intercept of a conversation between you and Rajko Djukic on the 2nd March 1992, and you spoke about Mr. Djukic yesterday. And you told Mr. Djukic during this conversation that you have visited the check-points and Sarajevo is ours. Further down, Mr. Djukic stated: "This was a big test." To which you responded: "Definitely. It was a live practice." Mr. Stanisic, you considered the barricades a live practice for implementing the take-overs of the municipalities that followed in April and onwards. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not true. I can explain. Mr. Prosecutor, you see, the service monitored telephone conversations, but you can see that on the following day if somebody had participated in that the service would have removed that. Both conversations took place on the following day after the activities had taken place, and it is true when I answered Mr. Karadzic's questions, we did tour the check-points and everything, and we looked at everything that we thought of some benefit for ending the whole thing. And when you want to gain something, you have to be witty, you have to be humour -- to humour somebody if you want them to help you, and I suppose that that was the context of that conversation. I didn't want to quarrel with people whom I needed to help me. At the time when both conversations were recorded shows that that was on the second day, on the day when we actually inspected the site of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So your evidence is this conversation was just a joke.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was a very serious conversation. However, there was some witty connotations there because when you want to resolve something -- obviously, those of us who attended specialist training courses in the MUP, we also learnt about negotiation techniques that help you to get to an agreement. The other side needs to hear something good if you want to involve them in dealing with the problem and to be on your side.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stanisic please be asked to speak straight into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, did you hear message? Please lean forward when you speak so that the interpreters can understand you. And what about your conversation on the 2nd of March with Stojan Zupljanin in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you go on. If you read further, Mr. Stanisic, on this intercept, you can see, couldn't you, you said: "I think that we must sit down one day and analyse this thoroughly." And later on you said: "So that we do not make the same mistake next time." Do you see that passage? Which are your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just said to his question -- can you please bear with me? Can you direct me to the exact passage? Can you perhaps use the pointer to point it to me? When he says that he did something good and big, that a big thing was done, I added to that, We have to sit down and analyse this big thing, if it was, indeed, big.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see the passage where you said: "Da drugi put ne bi kiks"? So it's -- I don't know, but "We do not make the same mistake next time." Do you see that point? Do you see the pointer? Cursor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I can see it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you mean by the "mistake"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the whole context and the line of thinking can be seen from the first two or three sentences. First he said that they had done a big thing. Then I interjected and I said, If a big thing has been done we have to analyse it so as to avoid any failures in the future. But I spoke in a humorous way, as it were. I wanted to achieve a goal. I didn't want to dwell upon the matter for too long. I wanted to water down the conversation and come to the way the problem could be resolved by wielding their own influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stanisic. My question was what this same mistake referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To what he previously said, that a big thing has been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it at that. Yes, please continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's try to have P5597 on the screen. See if this clarifies matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now what we're going pull up is a telephone intercept again on the 2nd of March of a conversation between you and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 2 of the English, page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You told Mr. Zupljanin: "Now be ready and we'll be in touch." To which Mr. Zupljanin responded: "We are waiting for the sign. If a total blockade is needed or the rest, it will be done." To which you responded: "Agreed."

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Stojan Zupljanin had on his mind. I know that there was a conversation that they had stopped three or four trucks full of weapons that were entering Banja Luka and were intended for the HDZ. I know that we discussed that in a conversation. And I told him that we had to be very careful and cautious with this regard, but I really can't remember what this -- I believe that in Banja Luka on the 1st of March, there were no barricades at all, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Are you meaning to tell us that on the 2nd of March, when a major barricade incident is going on in Sarajevo, you were having an entirely unrelated conversation with Mr. Zupljanin down in Banja Luka about a blockade in that town. Is that what you're telling us, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if there was something specific in here, I could answer your question, but I really can't remember what kind of a conversation I had ten or twenty years ago. I really can't explain my own words uttered at the time. I wish I could help you, but everything would be mere speculation. I don't know what he meant. I remember that there was a conversation about some arms that entered Banja Luka or were supposed to enter Banja Luka. And then I spoke about blocking the border with Croatia because there was a war going on in Croatia. It was topical at the moment when those barricades were erected in Sarajevo, and that -- when there was some unrest in Sarajevo, but I don't think that there were any barricades erected in Banja Luka at the same time. I really can't say that for a fact. That was a long time ago. And I really can't make any good and proper inferences from what I see before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic then the answer should be, I don't know or I don't remember. You don't need to go through this thinking aloud for us because we need get through.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have P961 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, what I'm now going to show you is the stenograph of the 12th Session of the Assembly, the Bosnian Serb Assembly, held on the 24th of March, 1992. And this session was held on the same day that you were appointed minister of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 21 of the English, page 38 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is speaking and he states: "What is important to us at this moment is the minister of the interior, a regular and reserve police force of the size we would want" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Next page for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you, Your Honour. Your eyes are much better than mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: He goes on to say: "... a regular and reserve police force of the size we would want is also important because no one is limiting us in any international agreement on this point." Further on -- down says: "You with be sure that members of the police are quite sufficient. We have a legal basis in the Law on Internal Affairs, we have an insignia, and at desired moment and this will be very soon we can form whatever we want."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's next page for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic then continues: "At a given moment in the next three or four days there will be a single method used and you will be able to apply it in the municipalities you represent including both things that must be done as well as how to do them: How to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people, and take command. The police must be under the control of the civilian authority, it must obey it, there is no discussion about that ..." Mr. Stanisic, as the newly appointed RS MUP minister, you were aware, weren't you, of these plans to use the police to take command in the municipalities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, your conclusions are wrong. Let's go back to the first paragraph and let's take questions one at a time. That's the only way I can answer them. Let's go back to the part where Karadzic mentions the police. I want to be able to explain things to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, I asked you first to answer my question which is quite simple: The plan he is announcing with regard to taking command in the municipalities --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The plan Mr. Karadzic is talking about to take command --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- in the municipalities, can you please tell us: You were aware of those plan, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. I can't answer a question which contains three or four questions to which answers are different. Please ask one question at a time. You are starting from the first Karadzic's statement and this has nothing to do with your question. Let's go back to the previous page. Your Honours, may I be allowed to explain what that was all about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an assembly session. There were a lot of MPs present. When entities were being set up - and they insisted that besides the MUP, there should be a military or Serbian Guard or God knows what else - and Karadzic explained that according to the Cutileiro Plan, all we were allowed to have was the police within an entity and that was enough to establish power where entities were functional, that we did not need the military, and that the police was enough for natural disasters and things like that. And that was all that was needed in an ethnic area within a state, that the police would be enough, that we did not need the military or some sort of a guard. Now having said that, we can go on. You can now put your question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question is simply when Mr. Karadzic speaks about at a given moment in the next three or four days there will be a single method used, et cetera, et cetera, how to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people, and take command, you were aware of these plan, were you not, as the newly appointed RS minister? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Prosecutor. This was not a conclusion. This was a discussion which was taking place at the meeting. This was not a -- a conclusion that I received as a minister, and given to act upon that. This was a discussion, a debate, at an assembly meeting, and there were a lot of proposals heard during that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have P1116 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is -- what I'm going to show you is the dispatch from Momcilo Mandic, number 02-2482, dated 31 March 1992. And in this dispatch, Mandic announces that on the 1st of April, 1992, the CSBs and SJBs of the BiH MUP on the territory of the Serbian Republic of BiH are - and this is towards the bottom of the page in the English - "abolished and ceased to function and their authority are taken over by the organisational units of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of BiH." This is it -- the dispatch, Mr. Stanisic, that triggered the ethnic division of the MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Please. Let's clarify one thing. You see, within the scope of two days, first you -- you saw the discussion of Mr. Karadzic, and here the conclusions are completely different. In keeping with the constitution and the Law on Internal Affairs, and based on -- on the levels reached in the Cutileiro Plan, that transformation should have been carried out but within the centres and not in the municipalities as it was claimed just a while ago. In other words, that should have been done in keeping with the Law on Internal Affairs and the organs were supposed to agree on the transformation. It was not left to the municipalities, as we heard from Karadzic. And that's why I'm saying that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, this dispatch was sent not just to the CSBs but also the SJBs in the municipalities. This dispatch applied to the municipalities, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. It says very clearly: Within the scope of security organs and the Ministry of Interior of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina and later of Republika Srpska was a centralised body which had nothing whatsoever to do with municipal bodies. There were indeed public security stations but they were under the authority under the services centres, and those centres were under the authority of the MUP if everything was done by the book. And he says clearly here what needs to be done. He doesn't mention municipalities. It had to be done within the spirit of the Law on Internal Affairs. And it is true that on several occasions to all of us in the MUP of the joint state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we were familiar with the levels of agreement reached. We knew that the Cutileiro Plan had been as signed and that the principles of the constitutional organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be respected. But since there were tensions, and I told you just a while ago that I don't even like to remember those times, every village, every town had its own Home Guards that were outside of the framework of the Ministry of Internal affairs, and this should have been done in a positive spirit, that the -- everybody should know what the police forces were and that all the paramilitaries should withdraw from all the villages and towns both in the Serbian and in the Muslim part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Stanisic, a very, very long answer to a very simple question. Please try to regulate yourself to answer as briefly, as concisely as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 65 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll do my best, but it's very difficult to use just one word to deal with such complex topics as you're raising.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 25901 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What I'm about to show you, Mr. Stanisic, is a dispatch from the BiH MUP dated 1 April 1992. And if you could look at the first paragraph, the dispatch notes the absence of a certain number of employees from their posts as a result of Momcilo Mandic's dispatch 02-2482 of 31 March 1992 which we just looked at. The dispatch then states that the BiH MUP collegium requires the return of all MUP employees and their involvement in the execution of regular tasks. The members of the collegium signed this, even Momcilo Mandic, with the exception of you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this dispatch was a result of another dispatch, i.e., of a collegium meeting that was held before that. I'm sure that you have the minutes of that meeting and its conclusions. At that moment, President Alija Izetbegovic had learned that the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be recognised. He ordered the minister to abort everything, that Cutileiro's Plan should not be accepted, and, as a result of that, this dispatch arrived so Delimustafic was told to give up on Cutileiro Plan, to withdraw his signature, and that that was no longer valid, and then Alija sent this dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic my question was simply this was signed by the members of collegium with the exception of you. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, you -- in order to hear the simple answer, you should make your question simple as well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, and I'm -- certainly I'm trying. I appreciate the -- the reminder.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in the first paragraph, it's citing to Momcilo Mandic's memo of 31 March, isn't it? The one we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's clarify things. I'm just stating a fact, that that's what I'm reading. I don't know what he meant, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6631, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen, P2745.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask? When it comes to Mandic's and Kosoric's signatures, has their authenticity been established? Zepinic's signature I can perhaps say that it is his signature, but I don't know about the other two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It may go to the weight but we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P2745 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, this is a dispatch from you dated 3 April 1992. It was sent on the same date that you claim you met with Jusuf Pusina in your testimony yesterday. And if we could look at the first paragraph, it is evident that -- this is your response to the BiH MUP collegium dispatch that we just looked at; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What has my meeting got to do with this dispatch? This is a dispatch which I -- will you allow me to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No. Let me clarify my question for you so we can simplify this. My question is simply -- we see the first paragraph and it references a dispatch that was sent out with Momcilo Mandic's signature. First of all, it says -- in the English translation it says sent out on behalf of the Serb Republic of BiH MUP. In fact, it's the Socialist Republic BiH MUP, isn't it, SRBiH?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear with me. I need to read this. It's the second paragraph, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No. No, it's just the first paragraph, I believe. And there's a reference to -- it says in the original that you're looking at: "MUP SRBiH." That stands for the Socialist Republic of the BiH MUP; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's highly unlikely, because the name was the Serbian Republic and it could be confused with the socialist republic, so we need to ... look at it more carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the reason I suggest that is if you read on further --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know, yes. Go ahead, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Because if you read on further, you reference that the dispatch spoke about the return of all MUP employees -- yeah, to return to their regular jobs and tasks. That was the dispatch that we just looked at from the collegium; isn't that correct? That's what you're referencing.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this dispatch was a result of the information that was sent to me by Momo Mandic. He told me that the dispatch had been sent to the units in -- on the ground as -- alleging him as the author and he had nothing whatsoever to do with that dispatch. He said, "I just warned them to adhere to the regulations and laws. I wanted to keep the order. I wanted to told them not pay attention to all this -- all sorts of political disinformation and various connotations that were addressed to various organs, not only the Ministry of Interior." I told him not to pay heed to any dispatches or instructions which were not official but rather that they should act in keeping with the laws and regulations. That was the gist of that message.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we look at the second paragraph it's quite clear that you're telling your subordinates, the CSBs and SJBs, to essentially disregard the dispatch, the collegium dispatch that we just looked at, the one that was signed by the collegium with exception of you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. It's not about the dispatch. It says here, "We inform you that on the 3rd of April, 1992, on behalf of Serb Republic of BiH MUP, a dispatch was sent on behalf of Momcilo Mandic, inviting all OUP employees to return to their regular jobs and tasks." I repeat, this was just a common way people were being disinformed. Momo Mandic was called by somebody and informed about that dispatch, and he told me that he had never sent a dispatch of that kind. That's the gist of my message, that there was lot of disinformation and that they should adhere to the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the laws and regulations, and the orders that the Serbian part of the ministry received from me. This was to avoid any possible disinformation and to avoid instilling unrest among the personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, just for the record, it's our position that the SRBiH MUP that's referenced in the first, that stands for Socialist Republic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are following that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We saw many similar mistranslation like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have D4272 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What you're going have before you, Mr. Stanisic, is your letter that you were shown yesterday from the 18th of April, 1992. And this is the letter that you testified that you wrote because you felt you were duty-bound to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 2 of the English. We can stay where we are on the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In this letter you write: "Although only 18 days have gone by since the establishment of the MUP, it employs 4.000 active workers and several tens of thousands of reserve policemen who are controlling nearly 70 per cent of the territory of the former BiH." So, Mr. Stanisic, approximately a month before the establishment of the Bosnian Serb army, your police were already controlling most of the territory that became the Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, please, let me clarify one thing. This is still -- well, for the most part. Perhaps there was an incident or two. But the situation was peaceful. What I wanted to say here was that in a territory that was nearly 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that's where the Serb people live, which does not mean that there are lots of them in that area. I proceeded from the following: Almost 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina is land held by Serbs and that's what I meant, this territory, almost 70 per cent is in -- well, that's the Serb MUP, and then there's no information on radio or TV about that MUP, and I asked for co-operation. That was the essence. There was no war at the time in this period when I wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in the weeks leading up to the creation of the VRS, which, I believe, was on the 12th of May, 1992, the police continued to play a key role in taking control of the area that was to become the Republika Srpska in municipalities such as Vlasenica, Ilijas, Kljuc, and other municipalities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not correct. May I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you can do so briefly.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know very well that there was no Army of Republika Srpska but there was the Territorial Defence of Republika Srpska and that grew into the Army of Republika Srpska. So these were reserve soldiers from the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the function of the Territorial Defence and they had already been mobilised by the JNA; and that is to say, that they were the army in that area. And, that is to say on 14th, 15th of April, I think, when Republika Srpska, after -- I'm sorry. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think it was the 9th of April that a state of emergency was declared, then Republika Srpska declared it on the 15th of April, a state of emergency, and ordered that the Territorial Defence be mobilised as an armed force in Republika Srpska. That is the same Army of Republika Srpska where Commander Mladic came and some other generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mention mobilisation and yesterday you mentioned that Mr. Karadzic, in a state of emergency, had powers to determine the use and numbers of the police. It's correct, isn't it, that Mr. Karadzic ordered the mobilisation of the police force in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government makes proposals and the president of the state -- well, in 1992 in April there was a presidency. Karadzic wasn't president yet. It was Biljana and Koljevic. I just spoke about the institution of the president, that that is the institution that has the authority to state the number of active-duty and reserve policemen in a state of emergency and to order how they would be used. I spoke of the institution of the president. And in May, until May in Banja Luka, it was only Biljana and Koljevic, and it was only in Banja Luka that Radovan was made president.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That may be the case. But, in reality, Mr. Karadzic is the one that made these decisions, isn't that correct, and not Ms. Plavsic or Dr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- well, until the month of May. Now I remember. Now I remember a decision on the establishment of prisons. It was made by Koljevic and Biljana Plavsic. I mean, the system of the judiciary was falling apart and then they decided that in the territory of Republika Srpska prisons be established and they signed that. I remember that because in my defence, I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let me show you your interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: 65 ter 25865. This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want to go to page 389 of your interview. That's English. Page 236 of the B/C/S. And when you were asked whether Dr. Koljevic considered Karadzic to be the public leader of the Bosnian Serbs, you responded --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I please take a look?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Certainly, I apologise. I think it is -- yes, the one that's been zoomed in. And you were asked whether Dr. Koljevic considered Mr. Karadzic to be the public leader of the Bosnian Serbs, and you responded: "I know that was Karadzic and Krajisnik who made the decisions and actually had the final word." That was the situation throughout the existence of the Bosnian Serb Republic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, a moment ago by way of a foundation of your question, you asked me about the declaration of emergency, whether it was Karadzic. I said it was the president. Anybody. Whoever may be president irrespective of the name concerned. And nobody asked me here about the president. They asked me here about leaders. The state function of the president is one thing and a leader is another thing. It is true that the socialist democratic -- no, the Serb Democratic Party was then the party in power and the leader of that party was Mr. Karadzic, not Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Objection. Now, in the Serbian please could it be clarified with the witness. Does it say "zavladao" or "zalago" [phon]? So if the Serb transcript is wrong, then that is really something. Could that please be clarified. So it is line 3 and line 5. It says "zavladao" and obviously it was "zalago."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where are we in terms of English?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think he is referring to the -- well, Mr. Karadzic will have to point us in the right direction, but I think it's at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In B/C/S. But in English? Who is VK? I don't ... No, top of the page in B/C/S, we see.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think VK is the interpreter. Well, I might be wrong. I'd have to look at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But where do we have it in the English? Previous page?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the previous page, if we could. And then go to the bottom. I don't see it there. I don't see VK.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's there. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it translated as TS: Established? I don't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that wasn't the page I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it was not referred to by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And I seek to tender the page that I did refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 359.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will add that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 389, yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Is the Serbian page also following this? Because the transcription is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether correct B/C/S page was shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think the one that's currently on the screen is the one because -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do we have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Actually, let me check.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What? Which part? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think the part that I read out was towards the bottom. We see AT, that's Mr. Tieger. And it starts out with Koljevic and then it continues, and then Mr. Stanisic gives his answer. I think that's the part I read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that the part which was a part of Mr. Olmsted's question is the -- is the ultimate paragraph from this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But what Mr. Karadzic is talking about is the very first and the second line on -- on this same page. And the problem appears to be that in the English text that is the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The first and the second line are on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have 65 ter 10838 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is the interview for the Javnost that you provided on 30th of October 1992 which was tendered through you yesterday. And if you could look -- and I'll do my best at this. But it's page 2 of the English, and I believe it's the first column towards the bottom of the page. And I'm interested in the part where you state: "Fortunately, the Ministry of Interior indeed functions as a centralised organ ... also it has not happened yet that anyone in the whole territory of the Republika Srpska ever refused to carry out any of my orders, issued, of course, in accordance with the law."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then if we could go to page 3 of the English, and this is, I think, at the bottom of the second column --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could the page be put down, because this part, in Serbian, is not visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can look at the second column at the bottom, I believe, of the B/C/S, and we're on page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You stated during this interview: "The burden of defence was carried by the milicia," presumably meaning the police, "and the Serbian people. Thanks to a good organisation and commitment we then managed to set up most of the borders as they are today." Mr. Stanisic, that was your description of the organisation of the RS MUP in 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just show me the dates so that I could see when this interview took place? May I explain? This is an interview on the 30th of July, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that is to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not 30th of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I think it's 07 ... or October. October. I don't see it here. But the essence is -- let me just say this: I gave this interview to a newspaper and, you see, rather late in 1992 regardless of what the date is. After the arrest of paramilitary units from Serbia in the territory of Republika Srpska and, how do I put this, through my interview, I wanted to issue a threat saying that we were strong, that they should not come, that we would deal with all of those who would come. The essence is the organisation and everything that was there, but I felt duty-bound after rather successful operations, because criminals don't know whether the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia helped us or not, and that is why I presented all of this as if it were our own, that were organised, that we would arrest everyone, that everything would be in accordance with the law. If any crimes are committed, nothing else would be done but that. And most of the members of the Ministry of Interior at first did take part in various combat operations. However, they were resubordinated to the Territorial Defence or the Army of Republika Srpska or even in a certain part the JNA, if they were present. You see, there is not a single document of mine that has to do with ordering combat operations, activities, et cetera, because, after all, I'm not knowledgeable about that at all. And it is true that most members did take part. There were quite a few casualties but in the way that I explained it just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, did the witness agree with your interpretation that milicia meant police?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you referred to milicia you meant police; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant members of the Ministry of Interior. Somebody calls them milicia, somebody calls them policija.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 65 ter 26979 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It hasn't been released, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, one of your first acts as minister --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in fact, if we could pull up on the screen 65 ter 25902.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: One of your first acts as minister was to appoint your five CSB chiefs: Mr. Zupljanin, Mr. Jesuric, Krsto Savic, Andrija Bjelosevic, and Mr. Cvijetic, isn't that correct? That was one of your first acts as minister.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of those whose names were mentioned were members of the Ministry of Interior until then and almost all of them held the same positions, and I just issued decisions to link up years of service. Many people I did not even know, the persons that I issued this to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're looking at Mr. Jesuric's appointment. You knew him; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jesuric was chief of the public security station in Bijeljina and it was Alija Delimustafic who appointed him. I just issued a decision in order to have continuity so that his service would not be interrupted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I believe that it would be very helpful if the Prosecutor would put complete questions. If the question has to do with appointments, he should say temporary appointment because that is what it actually does say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure it matters at all, but -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting. Yes. If I misspoke -- the document speaks for itself, let's say that. If this may be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain? May I clarify? If it is in the interest of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it's temporary or not, why does appointment matter at all at this stage? I don't think it's challenged at all. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6632, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Early in the conflict you organised the police into war units; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at P2966.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what's going to be on the screen is an order by you dated 15 May 1992, and I'll repeat my question: You established -- you organised the police into war units; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my obligation according to the law, the law of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, is based on the Law on National Defence. I think it is paragraph 3, where there's a reference to the tasks of the police; milicia, in war time. So we were supposed to make a plan of defence preparations within our ministry. Since all members of the Ministry of Interior had served in the military, there was no professional army before the war. All men of military age had to do their military service. So then, according to that law, they were members of the army. So a member -- every member of the Ministry of Interior had to have done his military service before that, and this was still the situation, when necessary. When the president is supposed to order the use, then the ministry has to be organised according to their military assignments, the VS, et cetera. How they are organised in peacetime, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, this time your answer could have been simply yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just wait. There's a translation all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we continue or shall we take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, perhaps this is a time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olmsted. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have on the screen 65 ter 18287.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stanisic, before the break we were talking about the war units that were established within the RS MUP police force. And what have you in front of you is a 6 July 1992 document issued by you regarding some basic principles of the MUP when applying war-time procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could look at page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under Roman numeral III, you wrote: "Conditions for successful operation while implementing war-time procedures ...," and you included "organisation of the police and other MUP services into war units, some of which carry out regular duties and carry out specialist operative duties on the ground (neutralising sabotage and terrorist groups, organised criminal activities of the armed individuals, and so on, in co-operation with the Serbian army) ..." That's correct, Mr. Stanisic, isn't it, that these war units functioned both in combat operation but also as special police units?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please show me what you are alluding to. I'd like to read it, because I didn't. What paragraph do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's under Roman numeral III, and I believe it is the...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance. It's the -- it's the very last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, once again, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I don't think -- previous page. The last paragraph on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stanisic, I just read it out to you, and my question - and I'll repeat for you - is, that these war units that --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could this please be blown up just a little? The letters are just too tiny. Go ahead then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question to you is: That these war units that you established within the police force, they performed both combat operations as well as specialist operative duties which fall within the typical duties of a special police force; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when those units were not engaged in military tasks, they were engaged on the tasks pertaining to the Ministry of Interior. As can you see here, none of these are military tasks. At the moment when an order was received to resubordinate them to the military, then, together with the military, they were engaged on military duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before doing that, I didn't follow your question. What's the distinction between combat operation and specialist operative duties? What you did mean when you put that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was actually reading from the document, but I think it will be appropriate for the witness to explain the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where do you have combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Oh. We've already talked about war units and that, as the witness has mentioned, that they did perform combat operations. That's not in dispute. What I asked the witness is -- is that in addition to combat operations they also performed specialist duties, as described in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stanisic, do you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may help you to understand, I'd like to say that those were members of the Ministry of Interior. When they were under the authority of the ministry and when they were performing tasks pertaining to the Ministry of Interior, they were also under the authority of the minister of the interior officers. They could be engaged in combat on the order of the Supreme Commander or a person designated by him, and then they were resubordinated. But then they were also under the authority of those commanders who were in charge of the planning and the implementation of combat operations. Thank you very much. I hope I was of some assistance with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6633, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P2760 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is the RS MUP performance report for the period of April through June 1992. Mr. Stanisic, to whom were these reports submitted?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On every report, there should be a list of addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would they be -- would they be submitted to the presidency?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They contain a lot of information. And I suppose that some of the reports did if there was something interesting in the report or where the information might be of some interest to the presidency because they could be instrumental in dealing with the problems mentioned in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 9 of the English, page 15 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it's reported in this performance report that measures have been taken to ensure that all employees of Serbian nationality join the MUP? That's correct, isn't it, Mr. Stanisic, that measures were taken in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Join? To the largest extent, Serbian nationals joined the MUP. That's true. I don't know what the author meant. This is not my document. But it is true that most of the Serbian cadre did join the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You said this isn't your report, but you as RS MUP minister would have had to see this report and approve it; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't mean that. Reports were written by different people and sent to different bodies. If I was one of the designated addressees, then I must have received it or perhaps reports were sent to police administrations or particular Security Services Centres. They did not necessarily have to be addressed or sent to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So you're asserting that you, as minister, wouldn't have received the performance report of the RS MUP necessarily, that you wouldn't necessarily receive it? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. It doesn't say that anywhere here. I can see one page with a text. I'm telling you that there were various reports and they were sent to the designated addressees. If they were sent to the minister, it was also received by the minister but there were reports sent to various other levels. For example, police stations received them. If one of the addressees was the minister, then, of course, I would have received such a report, but I really can't remember. It was a long time ago. It is -- if it is indicated that this particular report was to be sent to the minister, then, yes, the minister did receive it. This page that we have on the screen does not help me in making the right references.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, the report continues to state that except for six employees of Muslim nationality - five in Kalinovik and one in Ljubinje - all other employees are of Serbian nationality. That is information that was available to you at the end of June 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Could you show me? I want to see which organisational unit drafted this report. I want to be able to give you a precise answer and then I can answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps we can turn to the first page and you can look at the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the heading: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ministry of Interior, Performance Report," but who is the author? Which organisational unit drafted this report? I can't -- I can't see that. And also, I can't see a list of addressees, who it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Regardless of who made this document, it states in it that except for six employees of Muslim nationality, all other employees are of Serbian nationality. And my question to you is: That's the information that you had at the end of June 1992. Putting aside this report, that's the information you had.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this alone, I cannot affirm that I was privy to this information. If you have something else, maybe this is just about one police station in Kalinovik or perhaps somewhere else. This does not reflect the entire situation in the MUP. That's why I need to know more than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 25903. And if we could turn to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You can see that you received this one; correct, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that. It doesn't say that I received it. But if you show me the entire document, if I see the contents, maybe I will remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, under "delivery" it says minister of the interior, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you're alluding to, I don't know. It does say so, but it doesn't say that I ever received it. Perhaps you can give me a moment to read the entire document. Or, actually, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'm simply establishing that this was delivered to you as -- it says in the English version at the very bottom, it says: "Delivery" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are repeating the same. It says it is addressed to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It doesn't say minister received this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We heard that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 2 of the English, and I believe it's page 1 of the B/C/S, it states: "All employees are Serbian except six who are Muslim." And that's at the top of the page. And I'll repeat, Mr. Stanisic, that is the information that you had in June 1992; correct.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Let me read the first paragraph. According to inconclusive and imprecise indicators, i.e., records that I maintained in the personnel affairs in the Ministry of Interior affairs -- internal affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of age -- in 1992, the ministry has 1.831 employees, and this information does not contain data on the Banja Luka centre, so I can't give you that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'd like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6634, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could have P2761 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And this is the RS MUP annual report on the work in period of April through December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 27 of the English, page 38 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. I apologise. When was this report drafted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I believe at the bottom it says January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993 I was not in office. I was not minister. However, if you allow me to read the contents of the document, maybe I will be able to help you with the document. I didn't receive it because at the time I was no longer in office. But I'm willing to help you, if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I appreciate that and let me ask you a question. I think we have page 27 up on the screen. It says: "In implementing personnel policies, the starting points were primarily Serbian patriotism and professionalism ..." Now, we'll talk about professionalism in a minute. But listed first as a criterion of personnel policy of the RS MUP was Serbian patriotism; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have P1105 on the screen. And this is returning to the 22nd Session of the RS Assembly on 23rd of November, 1992. And if we could turn to page 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Where somewhere in the midst of your speech at this session, in which you state: "In the beginning, we did that because there were reserves in the police. We wanted the country defended, so they took on thieves and criminals because I tell you not a single doctor picked up a rifle to defend his country. Not a single intellectual. Our priority, our intentions were good, and maybe that is where we went wrong. Maybe that is where I went wrong. Agreed. But in that case, I should be told clearly that is where you went wrong, sir, you can't do that. This is no longer a job for you." Mr. Stanisic, it wasn't the SDA or HDZ that brought the thieves and criminals into the police force of the RS MUP, as you suggested yesterday. They made it into the police force because you wanted them there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must object. And I'm -- I'm -- I have to intervene at this point, and I would like -- like you to compel Mr. Stanisic to answer this question. Because the issue is very alive in -- in the appeals proceedings against him. And -- and there is a reasonable probability that he might incriminate himself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, do you agree with Mr. Zecevic, that you are going to refuse to answer this question on the ground that it might incriminate you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, may I be heard on the issue on whether you should compel the witness to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's our position that you should not compel the witness to answer this question. As the Appeals Chamber has said, you have to balance the right of the parties to have sufficient information concerning this case with his own right in his case. And I think, therefore, that only the most central issues relating to this trial and the witness's credibility ought to be those which you use to compel his testimony. And I don't think, given what's already in the document, that asking him about whether he approved reserve police officers who were less than qualified is so central to the case that you should compel him to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, do you like to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Nothing from us, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be heard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I disagree with my learned friend, Mr. Robinson, on this matter because the -- the essence of the Rule 90(E) is to protect the interests of the witness. Therefore, whether this issue is -- is central to this case has no -- no relevance in respect to the witness's interests, which are protected by 90(E). Therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what -- I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Zecevic. What -- which is -- is interests of the witness? To compel him or not compel him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the interest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He refused to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The interest is to compel him to testify, Your Honour, to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Respecting his refusal is also -- would also be in the interests of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely it will be. But I -- it is my understanding that -- that the witness -- that the witness will be -- will be willing to provide Your Honours, to assist Your Honours, with the answer, if he is guaranteed the protection by 90(E), yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stanisic, the Chamber has decided to compel you to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can you then put your question to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, I read what you said during the 22nd Session of the RS Assembly. And I put to you that it wasn't the SDA or HDZ that brought criminals into the RS MUP reserve police force, which is what you suggested yesterday during your testimony. Rather, I put to you they made it into your reserve of police force because you wanted them there. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not correct. As I stressed already, when I say "we," on occasion, I mean the Serb side, but I say here specifically that they took on thieves and criminals, I would have said "we took them," but I said "they" took them on board, including thieves and exactly what I said yesterday. In any case, I do not exclude the possibility that in certain war-time police stations, crisis staffs and the like, they took such people on board, but it was not under MUP control. I had sent clear instructions out into the field as to who could become a member of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 16 -- 15, actually. As I stressed before, when I say they brought them on board, not we, as the Serb side. The sentence should have a different meaning. Lines 15 to 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The transcript say "we as Serbs," meaning Serbs are addressed as "we," and "they" didn't mean to be Serbs. That's my understanding. Do you agree, Mr. -- but could you assist us, if you could repeat your answer, Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me cut it short to make it clear. This should be read -- well, I read in the Serbian what I said. I said they brought in thieves and criminals too. That is what I mentioned yesterday. I do not exclude the possibility -- actually, there were specific cases where Crisis Staffs, in the war-time police stations they had established, employed people contrary to my instructions. And we had to fight that as well, to get rid of them, and can you see that in a whole number of orders I issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But it also says or you also said during the speech: "That is where I went wrong. Agreed. But in that case, I should be told clearly." Unlike today, Mr. Stanisic, back then you were taking responsibility for that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, following this complete thought, there's a comma, and then I say perhaps there is my fault in some of it too. Because it didn't only touch upon that specific topic. We discussed a number of things, and then I asked if there's anything that would be my fault, please tell me what it is. This was not the only thing discussed at the session. That is why the comma. Then I stressed well perhaps some of the blame may be mine, and if it is, do tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's bring in -- up on the screen, P1478.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stanisic, this is one of the diaries by General Mladic. And it was admitted into evidence in your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 337 of the English, page 371 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now this describes a meeting on the 27th of July 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's not before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is -- describes a meeting on the 27th of July, 1992, that you attended along with General Mladic, as this is his diary, and Milan Trbojevic. And during this meeting it's recorded in his notes that you stated: I had to take everyone into the police, but the army has now taken over all the lines. Mr. Stanisic -- do you see that, Mr. Stanisic? Do you see where it is written --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that is what it reads. Sorry. This was copied from Mladic's diary as you mentioned, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Exactly. This is from Mr. -- or from General Mladic's diary. Now when you refer to "everyone," you were including thieves and criminals; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, these are not my words. I told Mr. Mladic the very same thing I said at the assembly, but he cut it short. There are only a few words here, and he was probably interested in what I was trying to achieve rather than something else. But I told him the very same words I uttered at the assembly meeting. These are not my words. This is what Mr. Mladic noted down. It is correct that there were all sorts of people in the Ministry of Interior at the beginning of my mandate, but it wasn't the Ministry of Interior. It was the very inceptions of a ministry, and we had to clean up the mess we found. That is what I told Mladic. He simply summarised it and it turned out this way. What I was trying to warn him here was what the situation was like; whereas, the situation at the moment was quite clean. Things were tidied up, and we could responsibly approach our tasks and duties in our fight against unlawful conduct and their perpetrators -- and its perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now this reserve police force that included thieves and criminals, it was used to a significant extent to round up and detain large numbers of non-Serbs throughout the RS in 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I received some initial information during the collegium meeting in Belgrade in terms of who was included as stated in the report I sent to the president, pertaining to the meeting of the collegium. Probably there were some, although I didn't know who there was at the time, but probably there were and for that reason my first measure was to tidy up the MUP so that it can go about its own work. If someone has criminal intentions and is a criminal, I can't ask them to do police work. That is why there's a number of orders of mine which were implemented by my inspectors whom I sent in the field. We tried to clean things up first in order to be able to approach our job properly because one can't work with such people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it wasn't just the 11 July 1992 collegium meeting at which this issue of police being employed at these detention facilities arose, but also --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could P1097 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It was also raised in Mr. Zupljanin's dispatch to you which we'll look at in a moment. This is the dispatch and he writes that the representatives of the army and police arrested great number of citizens of Muslim and Croat nationality who were, depending on the number and the circumstances in the field, sent to various buildings. And he goes on to say, Mr. Stanisic, that among these detainees were persons of no security interest who can be treated as hostages. And if we look at, I think, the next page, he also mentions that among the detainees were elderly invalids and minors. Returning to the first page, he states that a large number of active and reserve policemen are engaged in securing these persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. Sorry. Let's stay with this page. Where does it say "hostages"? I need to remind myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be again of assistance, it's the first paragraph on the -- on this page, which is -- which we have on the -- on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, once again, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's clear one thing up. It doesn't say that they should be used as hostages, given that this seems to be the basis of your question. It is stated that they cannot be treated as hostages. One cannot treat people as hostages if there is no security-related information concerning them. There's no basis to hold them any longer. That is why I wanted to see it myself. Now I can proceed to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this is the first time this has ever been raised. This document was used in -- in Mr. Stanisic's case. I think this is an important issue, whether it says "can" or "cannot." It's our position it says "can" be treated as hostages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you ask the witness to read to out the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Because the paragraph is quite long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, could you read -- it starts with, "The third category is composed..." Can you read that full sentence, from "the third category"?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "While the third category comprises adult males for whom the service, until now, has not gathered any security-related information, due to which they can be treated as hostages." So the meaning was that they couldn't be treated, as such, until now. Not in the future. So the issue was how to treat them, since they were there, and, yet, there was no security-related information which concerned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really believe this is an issue that needs to be submitted to CLSS to get an accurate translation. We still disagree with what the witness has read out, and it's a very important issue that will need to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I would like the CLSS to take a look into this and report back as soon as practicable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add something else? There seems to be something missing just before the word "hostages." Maybe there's a word missing. Something seems to have been erased.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, the next paragraph, Mr. Stanisic, writes: "A large number of active and reserve policemen are engaged securing these persons." That was the case and you had that information, didn't you, Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, a moment ago, when I told that I received initial information on the 11th of July, you say that there was information I had had previously sent by Mr. Zupljanin. This is my response to the collegium conclusion and I asked for additional information so as to have a full picture to be ready for the meeting with the army commander, General Mladic, and the minister of justice, so that it can be dealt with. This is dated the 20th of July, whereas the collegium meeting was on the 11th. This is a response to the conclusion which I raised at the collegium meeting when I requested additional information. What they told me at the collegium meeting was insufficient in order for someone to gather all of them and -- all of it and submit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stanisic. And if I indicated this was sent to you before the collegium meeting, I did not intend that. But my point being, is that Mr. Zupljanin is alerting you that these detention facilities are a significant drain on police resources, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, these are our overall activities and efforts after the collegium meeting to deal with the problems. It is correct that there were problems and that we gave it our best at the time to deal with it, to the extent our competencies allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we may have P1096 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, this is the report that you conveyed to Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Djeric in which you provided some information regarding the police role in the detention facilities, as well as the inhumane conditions at those facilities. First of all, will you agree that nowhere in this report do you advocate that the detention facilities should be closed down?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, a moment ago I explained there's a conclusion from the collegium meeting. This information is a result of the collegium meeting. I was tasked with sending that initial information to the prime minister and the president, although that information was incomplete. In the conclusions of the collegium meeting, I requested that additional information be sent in so as to -- as for the presidency to undertake its own measure within its competence and the MUP to do its own work. At the collegium meeting, some urgent measures were indicated as well which could be tackled immediately. So this a result of overall activities to have those centres eliminated. If you recall that order of mine, I called them informal camps and I wanted us as the police to do as much as we could. And President Karadzic tried to exert his influence on the army. Irrespective of the fact that part of the reserve force provided security, if there was army personnel involved it fell under the competence of the army and we couldn't deal with it. That is why I sent such initial information to the addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm cognizant of the time. And at this time, perhaps I should make an application of additional time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much do you need? How much more do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well -- yes, let me see if I can calculate that very quickly. I would like -- I would ask for an hour and 15 minutes and let me tell you why, Your Honours. I have a number of topics I need to cover, finishing up with the detention facilities but also dealing with what the witness has testified generally about investigation of war crimes, as well as, you know, the priorities of his police to investigate crimes regardless of the ethnicity of the victims or perpetrators. And I did also want to touch on Koricanske Stijene as well as a couple of other, I think can be, fairly short matters, including paramilitaries which was also raised during direct examination in a very cursory manner, but nevertheless the witness did provide some general assertions regarding paramilitaries and how he was dealing with the problems. And one of the reasons I believe that -- this -- this case -- it's warranted as I have been receiving some fairly long answers here. I've really attempted to ask as precise questions as possible, and maybe I haven't succeeded in that in every capacity, but I have received a lot of long answers that I could not have anticipated. And I've also had to go -- resort to this witness's interviews and other documents that I didn't necessarily anticipate that I would have to in order to clarify matters. And so that has taken a lot more time than I anticipated. And I believe that in order for the Trial Chamber to fully understand this witness's evidence, that I need to cover these additional topics, and therefore I very respectfully request that I be given an hour and 15 minutes to wrap up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I ask? Is it a mistake? Is it 15 minutes or an hour and 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm asking for an hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your time will be up in five minutes and then you will have an extra hour, from then. So you have an hour and five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I appreciate it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, it was the case, wasn't it, that Mr. Karadzic received information about the facilities -- the detention facilities from the military; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can suppose so. I wasn't included in the chain of passing information. The military chain. We were a separate chain in the Ministry of Interior. In any case, they were duty-bound to inform their Supreme Commander, but I don't know to what extent they did so and whether they did in the first place. I can't go into that. In any case, they should have respected their chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at your interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 25865. And if we could have page 427 on the screen. And that page number is in the English version. In the B/C/S version, if we could have page 263.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, could you kindly repeat the English page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, the English is page 427.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stanisic, during the interview, you were being asked about the information you were providing pursuant to the requests of Mr. Kalinic who was the minister of health for the RS regarding detention facilities. And you state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we on the same page? I mean B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I believe so. Because I see Kalinic's name there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. If I can anticipate, that -- that it's line 20 in Serbian. That's where it starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yeah, I believe so. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you answered: "Because they were in possession of information from the army that the Presidency received on a regular basis. And what they wanted was to cross-compare, cross-check that information with any other source of information that they could obtain from the area.
