"Only that the army was fulfilling its obligation and was informing the Presidency on a regular basis which I can see from the documents submitted to me." That's correct, Mr. Stanisic, isn't it, that the army was supplying Mr. Karadzic with information regarding the detention facilities and the police were simply cross-checking that information or supplementing it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that sense. If I may, I'd like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you can do so briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it is the minister of health and Biljana Plavsic as a member of the presidency who were in -- who were tasked to communicate with the Red Cross, sign agreements, and make arrangements - the International Red Cross, that is - asked the MUP to carry out checks in the field, to provide additional information so that they would not provide incorrect information in their contacts. I accepted it because it was in our interest to gather that information for the police to do intelligence to the extent possible and I sent out orders. I did stress, however, that it was not within the competence of the MUP and the information provided needed to be cross-checked. I supposed the army was duty-bound to regularly report the -- to the Presidency, including Ms. Plavsic. So I discuss Kalinic and Mr. Plavsic here. And I still hold the opinion I was duty-bound to forward the information I had and so the army had to do the same. Anything beyond that is difficult for me to say. It would be speculation. That is why the ministry was included. And although it was not within our competence, within our authority, I ordered the state security members of the MUP to gather their own information so as to arrive at the truth. It was a difficult time. There was some incorrect reporting from all sides, and that is why it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this into evidence, but if we could have pages 426 to 427 be admitted, I think that will give a little more context to Your Honours when you're reviewing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you like. You can show the document -- those pages to the witness. Otherwise we'll admit this page -- we'll add this page only at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's just turn back one page then in the English and I suppose also in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stanisic, my question is simply is: This line of questioning was relating to information concerning the various detention facilities throughout the RS; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What is the line of questioning? What you are asking me or the interview or?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In the interview at this point in time, I just want to make sure it's clear that what you were answering was a question concerning information concerning detention facilities. And we can see this on this page where Mr. Tieger is asking about gathering data on captured Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It can be seen from my order that this is not under our authority but that they should do their best to collect intelligence in order to send this to the addressees that were read out here a moment ago so that they could compare what they have to this in order to be able to give information to the Red Cross that would be as accurate as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could tender those two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will add them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if we could have 65 ter 32824 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stanisic, you were a ware that non-Serbs were being arrested, held, and mistreated at detention facilities as early as April 1992, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Show me. I don't know. I cannot remember such a case. Or perhaps there were was some individual case I cannot remember. Show it to me. Show me where you are getting this from, and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So we have in front of us a telephone intercept of a conversation between you and Radomir Kojic from 18 April 1992. What position did Mr. Kojic told in the RS MUP at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kojic was in the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Pale. I cannot remember exactly now. I know that later he was battalion commander in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kojic tells on page 1 that Zoka is in Sokolac. He arrested all of those who were messing up with the weapons up there. And if we look on page 2, you respond: "So be it." Mr. Kojic then informs you: "He is arresting them and I, actually we agreed that he brings them to Vrace and hand them over there. They can beat them, they can do whatever they fucking want, and then we will move them, because we have no space here." To which you respond: "Fine." Mr. Stanisic, this conversation relates to non-Serb prisoners, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say that? Read it out to me that the detainees are non-Serbs? What is the foundation for that question of yours? I haven’t read that anywhere here that there were non-Serb prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I -- Mr. Stanisic, I'm putting it to you that these were non-Serb prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does the witness have the -- that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It should be page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm he does. It's on the screen, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question is, Mr. Stanisic, I acknowledge that there's no mention here of the ethnicity of the persons arrested, but I'm putting to you that they were non-Serb prisoners. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. And you're probably claiming that incorrectly because you do not have -- well, Your Honours, I can explain what this is all about, if the Chamber is interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Sokolac, the municipality of Sokolac is 95 per cent Serb populated, especially in the inner circle of Sokolac. This is what this is all about. From a barracks, Pofalic, that was close to the separation line. The weapons of the Territorial Defence of Sokolac there were, and then these weapons were withdrawn into Sokolac because it had been unprotected. Until then, it was the JNA that had secured that. When they brought that to Sokolac, then this -- these weapons were being abused and stolen, by the Serbs at that. These Serbs were arrested, taken to prison. I think they were prosecuted; I don't know. This was later handled by the public security station of Sokolac. So this really has nothing do with prisoners of war or non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are tendering this intercept between Mr. Stanisic and Kojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Did I miss something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are other conversations, so we'll admit this part.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6635, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have P1087 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, you were a member of the National Security Council; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When? Which period?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I believe the National Security Council came into existence around the -- in April of 1992 and continued until about June 1992, if my memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the office I held, and on the basis of the decision made by the assembly at the end of March, beginning of April, the minister of the interior was a member of the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can stay on page one of the English but turn to page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stanisic, what you have in front of you is the minutes from the National Security Council and government meeting held on 24 April 1992. And I want to draw your attention to the decision that states: "The Ministry of Justice shall take over the exchange of prisoners once the organs of the interior have completed their work." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that. Where is it? I haven't found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I can assist again. It's -- it's the second paragraph on -- on the page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And my question for you, Mr. Stanisic, is that that was the procedure that existed at the time. First, the minister -- Ministry of Interior completed their work with prisoners, and then they turned them over to the Ministry of Justice for exchange; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I explain? I think this is a concrete decision. We've talked about Vrace when two policemen were killed. These are responsible persons who organised that, and they were supposed to be interviewed in the context of the murder of these two policemen and then handed over to the Ministry of Justice. The intention was to have them exchanged because of tensions. However, the court was supposed to initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So it's your position, Mr. Stanisic, that this decision related only to two prisoners. Is that what your position is?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection. I don't remember anything else because at that time there weren't any others except for the persons that I'm talking about. Not that I know of, that is. These were not prisoners of war. These were suspects, murder suspects, for the murder of two policemen. Do you have something else that could remind me? It really was a very long time ago, and I cannot ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you're asserting that these murder suspects were simply exchanged in a population exchange; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the population. The Ministry of Justice took over, took over, continued proceedings. Where does it say "population"? Where is that written? I cannot see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The decision - and correct me if I have it wrong - states that the Ministry of Justice shall take over the exchange of prisoners once the organs of interior have completed their work. And I'm focusing on the word "exchange of prisoners." This deals with exchanging of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was defined here, but I know of that single case only. How they were treated at that moment. So it was the principal of the school and a few other suspects, murder suspects for the murder of those policemen. And then the Ministry of the Interior was supposed to conduct those preliminary interviews and then hand them over to the Ministry of Justice; that is to say, the prosecutor's office, the judiciary, and the Ministry of Justice as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have 1D50020 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is a report from SJB Novi Grad to the RS MUP under-secretary for public security dated 20 May 1992. Mr. Stanisic, who was the under-secretary for public security in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cedo Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it's reported to the RS MUP under-secretary that 156 persons are detained in KPD Butmir who were taken in custody on varies grounds by TO and JNA and preliminary operative interviews were conducted. And if we look on page 2 of the English, it is noted "the inadequate conditions of accommodation, food, hygiene, and state of health of detainees." Mr. Stanisic, the RS MUP had information about the inhumane conditions at detention facilities in May 1992, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. But this was not only submitted to Cedo, the under-secretary, but also to the Ministry of Justice. The Ministry of Justice too. Because they -- I mean the Territorial Defence, there was fighting going on, and during the fighting, as far as I can see here, these persons were taken prisoner and they were put up in the Kula prison, that is very close to Sarajevo, and the Ministry of Justice was informed about that and the under-secretary for public security was informed about that too. But -- I mean, it was the Territorial Defence that was involved in the fighting. And then they brought these persons into custody. However, adequate conditions existed only at the already-existing prison at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6636, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning of August 1992, you saw on television the international footage of the Prijedor detention facilities; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it possible that this is already admitted as P1126?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will check. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, let me repeat my question. At the beginning of August 1992, you saw on television the international footage of the Prijedor detention facilities, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, correct. But at the time, since we did not have electricity most of the time, on one occasion during the evening news there was a report but, of course, it was very brief, just by way of information. I think it was CNN or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could have D467 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'll repeat. If we could have Exhibit D467 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, despite all the information that was available to you regarding the detention facilities, the first and only order you issued to your police subordinates with respect to operating detention facilities at which non-Serbs were being detained was this 10 August 1992 order; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not correct. I sent several orders. That is to say, after the collegium in Belgrade, after the 11th of July, as a matter of fact, I repeated some. And I pointed out again, again, again -- probably not quite literally. I didn't just copy everything out. But energetically, I tried to exert pressure so that members of the MP would not have anything to do with the prisoners. In terms of persons who were brought into custody, they should only be treated on the basis of the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Law on the Interior. If there is a suspicion that they had done something, they can be kept for three days and then the prosecutor should be notified immediately as well as the investigating judge. That was the procedure at the time. And it is in that direction that I sent these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry let us read paragraph 2: "The security of collection centres shall be the direct responsibility of the Serbian army and if they do not have enough -- again, if they do not have enough personnel and they have involved reservists, then immediately they should be returned." And then the Secretariat for National Defence can deploy them in the army because we have no use for them. They are listed as members of the MUP and they are involved as members of the military and I pointed that out here, and we are not carrying out our duties and orders and that is why this order was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stanisic, we don't need you to repeat what the order says. But I put to you that your other orders or instructions regarding detention facilities, for instance, D450, which is the 19 July 1992 dispatch requesting information regarding detention facilities, D469 which is your 17 August 1992 dispatch regarding information about unofficial prisons which you looked at yesterday, and D475, which is your 24 August 1992 dispatch requesting information on behalf of the Ministry of Health, those all pertain to obtaining information. They were not orders with regard to what to do with the detention facilities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Mr. Prosecutor, you know that all these centres, I cannot be very specific now, but up until mid-September, the end of September, all of that was disbanded except for two POW camps that were under the control of the military. I think it was Manjaca and somewhere else. I don't know exactly. So the result of all of this pressure was the disbanding of these camps and indeed they were disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, you never ordered the disbandment of any detention facility at which non-Serbs were held; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, never was a single such centre established on the basis of any decision of mine or from the ministry. So those who set up the centres would have to disband them, and it was the Army of Republika Srpska that was involved in all of that. And that is why I informed the president, and through the army he did exert pressure and the Crisis Staffs that established these centres and then that was disbanded. I as minister of the MUP could not issue orders to the army or to the president of the municipality. As for that which was in my domain, that is to say, the Ministry of Interior, was separated from all of that on the basis of my orders and they managed. We managed to a large degree to set up a ministry of interior when we got rid of all of this municipal deadweight that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one last document, then I'm done with detention facilities. If we could have on the screen 65 ter 25981.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic, this is a dispatch from SJB Bosanski Samac to the RS MUP dated 28 November 1992. It's correct, isn't it, Mr. Stanisic, that as late as the end of November 1992 the police still had custody over non-Serb detainees; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO STANISIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I repeat: We did not manage to integrate the public security station until the end of 1992, and this was precisely in the context of establishing the public security station which was established by the MUP. And Andrija Bjelosevic, the chief of the centre, did have a lot of problems there. And we even sent a special unit from the MUP to help him in that. And it is true there were problems but they were resolved. And from then onwards once we established control over the public security station in Samac, these problems were no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6637, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I checked the record and I confirm, Mr. Karadzic, that Exhibit P6636 is a certified copy of Exhibit P1126. Therefore, we don't need to admit it separately and we'll vacate the number. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will assign this number P6636 to the Samac SJB document; i.e., 65 ter 25981. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of February, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.
